summary: Registers an ENUM service for SIP, focused on putting SIP addresses-of-record under telephone numbers. It follows RFC 3761 and was updated by RFC 6118.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3764 registers a service for the ENUM system, the DNS-based mapping from telephone numbers to internet addresses. The service it registers, E2U+SIP, says that the address found for a telephone number is a SIP address of record, the long-term name of a person rather than of a particular device.

subtitle: A registered ENUM service that maps telephone numbers to SIP addresses of record.

tldr.problem: ENUM can translate a telephone number into a URI, but the URI it produces has to say what kind of service it reaches. For SIP there was no registered enumservice, so a telephone number could not be mapped to a SIP address in a standard way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the E2U+SIP enumservice, which says that the resulting URI is a SIP or SIPS address of record, and explains why the service should point at an address of record rather than at a device address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3764 is a Proposed Standard from April 2004 and has been updated by RFC 6118.

today: RFC 3764 is a Proposed Standard from April 2004 and has been updated by RFC 6118. The E2U+SIP enumservice it registers is the standard way to publish a telephone number that points to a SIP address of record.

sections.title: Why an ENUM Service for SIP
sections.content:
ENUM, the E.164 Number Mapping system, uses the DNS to translate telephone numbers such as '+12025332600' into URIs such as 'sip:egar@example.com'. It exists mainly to interconnect systems that rely on telephone numbers with those that use URIs to route transactions. This document applies to the revised version of ENUM described in RFC 3761.

SIP, the Session Initiation Protocol, is a text-based application protocol that lets endpoints on the Internet discover one another to exchange context information about a session they would like to share. The sessions it sets up include Internet telephony, instant messaging, video and Internet gaming, and SIP can start a session involving several forms of real-time communication at once.
sections.plainLanguage: ENUM turns a phone number into an internet address using DNS. SIP is the protocol that sets up calls and chats over the Internet. This RFC registers a label that says a phone number maps to a SIP address.

sections.title: The Service Registration
sections.content:
The registration follows the template defined in RFC 3761. The enumservice name is E2U+SIP. The type is SIP, and no subtypes are defined. The URI schemes are sip: and sips:. The functional specification is section 4 of this document, the security considerations are in section 6, and the intended usage is COMMON.

The name follows the pattern of the ENUM family: E2U is the E.164 to URI resolution service, and the part after the plus sign says which kind of URI follows.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration is a short record. It gives the service a name, says the result is a SIP or SIPS address, and marks the service as one that is commonly used.

sections.title: Contact Addresses and Addresses of Record
sections.content:
The document specifies an enumservice field suited to SIP addresses of record, and distinguishes them from SIP contact addresses. A URI associated with a particular user agent, such as a SIP phone, is commonly known as a contact address. The RFC compares the difference to the difference between a device and its user. There is no formal distinction in the syntax of the two forms, but a contact address is tied to a particular device and may take a device-specific form such as 'sip:10.0.0.1' or 'sip:edgar@ua21.example.com'. An address of record represents the identity of the user, generally a long-term one, and does not depend on any device: users can move between devices, or be associated with several at once, while keeping the same address of record.

When a user agent creates a SIP request, it puts the address of record of its target in the To header field and, generally, in the Request-URI. The address of record of the sender fills the From header field, and the contact address of the device sending the request is listed in the Contact header field.

A SIP device can send a registration to a registrar on behalf of its user to associate its own contact address with the user's address of record, which makes the device eligible to receive requests sent to that address of record. The registrar then modifies the provisioning data in a SIP location service, creating a mapping between the address of record and the device where the user can currently be reached. When later requests arrive at the administrative domain of that location service, proxy servers ask the location service where to find the user and discover the registered contact addresses. A follow-me telephony service would use this availability data to find the best place to reach the user without trying every device. An address of record can also be registered with another address of record, so that a user at home can register their work identity under their home address of record.

When a SIP entity has to make a forwarding decision for a Request-URI that holds an address of record, it uses the mechanisms in the SIP specification to locate the resource, which ordinarily means resolving the domain part of the URI so the request can be routed to the proxy server responsible for that domain.
sections.plainLanguage: A contact address names a device, such as a phone at a particular address. An address of record names the person, and stays the same wherever they go. Registration ties the two together, so a call to the person's address finds the device they are using now.

sections.title: The E2U+SIP Enumservice
sections.content:
Traditionally the services field of a NAPTR record holds a string with two subfields, a protocol subfield and a resolution service subfield. ENUM defines an E2U resolution service, and this document defines E2U+SIP for SIP. The scheme of the URI that appears in the regexp field of a NAPTR record using this enumservice may be SIP or SIPS, and the enumservice is best suited to SIP addresses of record.

When a SIP address of record appears in the regexp field, there is no need to qualify the enumservice field with capability data, because addresses of record do not have capabilities. SIP user agents have specific communication capabilities, such as the ability to start a voice call with particular codecs or support for particular SIP extensions, but an address of record represents no particular device, so it has no capabilities of its own. When a user agent sends a request to an address of record, a phase of capability negotiation follows: the originating user agent first states its own capabilities and its preferences in the request, using SDP to list acceptable and favoured media, the Required and Supported headers to negotiate extensions, and sometimes optional SIP extensions such as callee capabilities. Proxy servers or endpoints then return responses, and the two sides negotiate in both directions.

The RFC contrasts this with what ENUM does. The process of negotiating capabilities can overlap with the main service that NAPTR records provide, which lets the originating client pick a URI from an ordered list of enumservices. But ENUM's capability management is one-way: the administrator of the telephone number states capabilities as protocol names and preferences, and the client evaluates them without negotiation. Listing available protocols is not the same as agreeing on session media down to the codec level or on extension support, and it would be hard to express the capabilities of a SIP device in that much detail inside a NAPTR service field. Provisioning contact addresses in ENUM rather than addresses of record would therefore compromise the SIP capability negotiation and discovery process, and if ENUM wanted to target particular devices, a service such as E2IPv4 would be more appropriate than E2U.

Two further points apply. A SIP address of record may use the SIP URI scheme or the SIPS URI scheme, and a SIPS URI in an address of record indicates that the user it represents can only be reached over a secure connection using TLS. And the user portion of a SIP URI may itself contain a telephone number, for example 'sip:+1442079460148@example.com', so clients should be careful to avoid infinite loops when they run ENUM queries again on URIs that came from an ENUM lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: The service says only that the address is a SIP address of record. It carries no capability information, because a person's address does not describe any device. The two ends of a call sort out codecs and extensions between themselves, and a client that runs ENUM on the result must not loop forever.

sections.title: The Example NAPTR Record
sections.content:
The example places a NAPTR record under the domain that holds the telephone number in the reversed numbering tree, with the service field set to E2U+sip and a regular expression that rewrites the telephone number into a SIP address of record:

$ORIGIN 8.4.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.4.4.e164.arpa.
IN NAPTR 10 100 "u" "E2U+sip" "!^.*$!sip:edgar@example.com!" .

The RFC also notes that there is generally no need for more than one NAPTR record under a single telephone number that points to a SIP address of record.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows the record that a number owner publishes: a DNS name built from the digits of the number, a service name that says SIP, and a rule that turns the number into a SIP address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A SIP address of record is the canonical address by which a user is known, so placing it in ENUM is comparable to placing an email address or a similar URI in the DNS.

DNS does not make policy decisions about the records it shares with an inquirer. All DNS records must be assumed to be available to every inquirer at all times, so the information in an ENUM record set has to be treated as open to the public, which raises privacy concerns.

Unlike a traditional telephone number, the resource identified by a SIP URI may require callers to provide cryptographic credentials for authentication and authorisation before the user is alerted. In that respect ENUM used with SIP can give far greater protection from unwanted callers than the existing telephone network, despite the public availability of the ENUM records. The RFC points to RFC 3761 for an analysis of the threats specific to ENUM's dependence on the DNS and the applicability of DNSSEC to them.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting a SIP address of record in the DNS is like publishing an email address: anyone can look it up. What the address leads to can still require credentials, which the telephone network does not do.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The document registers the E2U+SIP enumservice under the enumservice registry described in the IANA considerations of RFC 3761, with the details given in section 2.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list of registered enumservices, and this RFC adds one entry to it.
